name: Sell in May (Halloween indicator)

origin.source_title: The Halloween Indicator, Sell in May and Go Away: Another Puzzle (American Economic Review)

how_it_works.simple: Own stocks from November to April and sit in cash from May to October, because winter months have tended to be better.
how_it_works.analogy: Like a beach kiosk that only opens in the busy season and stays shut when few customers come.
how_it_works.precise: Bouman and Jacobsen document that stock returns from November to April exceed those from May to October across many countries. The strategy is a simple switch between equities and bills on fixed dates.

rule: On the last trading day of October buy an equity index fund; on the last trading day of April sell it and hold T-bills until the end of October.
economic_rationale: Bouman and Jacobsen call it a puzzle; suggested reasons such as summer vacations are untested in the sources read here.
why_it_might_fail: It gives up the summer equity premium: in the catalog's computation, May to October still averaged 0.75% a month in excess returns from 2003 to 2026, so the switch lagged buy and hold on a Sharpe basis (0.58 vs 0.72).

reported_results.source: Our calculation from Kenneth French data library, market excess return
reported_results.notes: Computed by the catalog on 2026-10-20 from the data file at source_url; this exact figure is not printed by the source. Arithmetic mean of monthly returns times 12; volatility is monthly standard deviation times sqrt(12); Sharpe uses excess returns; max drawdown from monthly compounding. Monthly returns compounded from daily data. Nov-Apr averaged 0.98% a month excess versus 0.42% for May-Oct. Always invested: Sharpe 0.46, max drawdown -84.7%.

post_publication_evidence: The seasonal gap persisted after 1998 in US data but shrank after 2002 (catalog computation from French data). Andrade, Chhaochharia and Fuerst (2013, https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v69.n4.4) titled their out-of-sample study 'Sell in May and Go Away Just Won't Go Away'; the catalog could only read the title, not the results. The catalog also could not open Bouman and Jacobsen's paper to quote their numbers.

relevance.reason: A simple timing rule versus the S&P 500; little direct link to FX.
